PASSO 1: no português, o “que” é o mesmo: STEP 1: English uses "who", "which" or "that" — and often drops the pronoun completely: "the man I know", "the book I read". German NEVER drops it: «der Mann, den ich kenne», «das Buch, das ich gelesen habe». STEP 2: look twice: the gender of the noun before it picks the family (der, die, das, die), and the job of the pronoun in its own clause picks the case — like English who (subject) vs whom (object).
The man who lives here is a doctor.
The man (that) I know is a doctor.
The woman who lives here is a doctor.
The woman (that) I know is a doctor.
The book (that) I read is good.
A oração relativa, passo a passo: The relative clause, step by step
PASSO 1: uma ORAÇÃO RELATIVA descreve um: STEP 1: a RELATIVE CLAUSE describes a noun: «Der Mann, der dort steht, ist mein Chef» (the man who is standing there is my boss). STEP 2: it starts with a RELATIVE PRONOUN that looks like the DEFINITE ARTICLE: der (m), die (f), das (n), die (plural). STEP 3: the GENDER and NUMBER of the relative pronoun come from the noun it describes (the antecedent): «Mann» is masculine → «der»; «Frau» is feminine → «die». In English "who" and "which" don't change — in German they do. STEP 4: the CASE of the relative pronoun comes from its job INSIDE the relative clause; in this lesson, it's the SUBJECT (nominative). STEP 5: the conjugated verb goes to the END of the relative clause, as with «weil» and «dass». STEP 6: the relative clause comes right AFTER the noun and between COMMAS — always, even where English uses no commas: «Der Mann, der dort steht, ist mein Chef.»
o português usa «que» para todos os gêne: English uses "who" for people and "which/that" for things, and the word order stays normal ("who is standing there"). German uses der, die, das, die for people AND things, never drops the pronoun, and sends the verb to the end: «der dort steht».
Der Mann, der steht dort, ist mein Chef.
Der Mann, der dort steht, ist mein Chef.
O verbo conjugado vai para o fim da rela: The conjugated verb goes to the end of the relative clause.
Der Mann der dort steht ist mein Chef.
A relative clause takes a comma before and after.
Die Frau, der dort steht, ist meine Chef: Die Frau, der dort steht, ist meine Chefin.
Die Frau, die dort steht, ist meine Chef: Die Frau, die dort steht, ist meine Chefin.
O relativo concorda com o gênero do subs: The relative pronoun agrees with the gender of the noun: «Frau» → «die».

Relativas com mais verbos, passo a passo: Relative clauses with more verbs, step by step
PASSO 1: a relativa pode ter qualquer te: STEP 1: a relative clause can be in any tense. Perfekt: «Die Frau, die gestern angerufen hat, ist meine Tante» (the auxiliary comes last). STEP 2: with a modal: «Der Student, der arbeiten muss, kommt nicht» (the student who has to work isn't coming). STEP 3: with a separable verb: «Der Zug, der um acht Uhr abfährt, ist voll» (the prefix rejoins the verb at the end). STEP 4: with «sein»: «Das Kind, das müde ist, schläft.» STEP 5: the main clause is "split" by the relative clause: «Der Mann, der dort steht, ist mein Chef» (the main clause continues after the relative clause, with its verb in second position of its own part).
Der Zug, der fährt um acht ab, ist voll.
Der Zug, der um acht abfährt, ist voll.

Usar relativas para identificar pessoas: Using relative clauses to identify people
PASSO 1: para IDENTIFICAR alguém, use a: STEP 1: to IDENTIFY someone, use a relative clause instead of a separate sentence: «Wer ist die Frau, die dort steht?» (Who's the woman standing there?) STEP 2: a relative clause can add several details: «Das ist Anna, die neue Kollegin, die seit Montag bei uns arbeitet» (that's Anna, the new colleague who's been working with us since Monday). STEP 3: relative clauses make your German sound natural and fluent: instead of «Das ist Paul. Er lacht immer laut.», say «Das ist Paul, der immer laut lacht.» STEP 4: careful: where English says "the woman standing there" with an -ing form, German needs a full relative clause: «die Frau, die dort steht».

Das ist der Mann, ___ dort wohnt.
O antecedente Mann é masculino e é sujei: The antecedent «Mann» is masculine and is the subject of «wohnt» in the relative clause. So the relative pronoun is nominative: der.
Das ist der Mann, ___ ich kenne.
Mann é masculino, mas na oração relativa: «Mann» is masculine, but in the relative clause it's the object of «ich kenne». «Kennen» takes the accusative: den (English: whom).
Das ist die Frau, ___ ich kenne.
Frau é feminino e objeto de kenne na rel: «Frau» is feminine and the object of «kenne» in the relative clause. The feminine singular accusative relative pronoun is «die» — the same as the nominative.
Das ist das Buch, ___ ich lese.
Das retoma Buch, neutro singular, como o: «Das» refers back to «Buch», neuter singular, as the object of «lese». It's a relative pronoun; «dass», with ss, is a conjunction and can't refer back to a noun.
Das sind die Leute, ___ im Haus wohnen.
Leute é plural e funciona como sujeito d: «Leute» is plural and the subject of «wohnen» in the relative clause. The nominative plural relative pronoun is «die».
A oração relativa den ich gesehen habe e: The relative clause «den ich gesehen habe» sits inside the main clause and must be set off by two commas in standard writing.
Na oração relativa com o modal müssen, o: In a relative clause with the modal «müssen», the infinitive «lesen» comes before the conjugated verb «muss»: das ich lesen muss.

Helfen rege dativo também na oração rela: «Helfen» takes the dative in a relative clause too. «Nachbar» is masculine singular, so the relative pronoun is «dem»: dem ich geholfen habe (whom I helped).
Das sind die Freunde, mit ___ (Dat. pl.): Das sind die Freunde, mit ___ (dat. pl.) wir in den Urlaub fahren.
Mit rege dativo. Como Freunde é plural,: «Mit» takes the dative. Since «Freunde» is plural, the relative pronoun is «denen»: mit denen wir in den Urlaub fahren. English can say "the friends we're going on vacation with"; German must put the preposition in front: «mit denen».
Das ist die Firma, in ___ (Dat. fem., wo: Das ist die Firma, in ___ (dat. fem., wo?) mein Bruder arbeitet, und da kommt der Bus, auf den (acc. masc., warten auf) ich warte.
In indica aqui o local onde o irmão trab: «In» here gives the place where the brother works and takes the dative. «Firma» is feminine singular, so the relative pronoun is «der»: in der mein Bruder arbeitet.
Das ist die Firma, in der (Dat. fem., wo: Das ist die Firma, in der (dat. fem., wo?) mein Bruder arbeitet, und da kommt der Bus, auf ___ (acc. masc., warten auf) ich warte.
Warten auf rege acusativo. Bus é masculi: «Warten auf» takes the accusative. «Bus» is masculine singular, so the relative pronoun is «den»: auf den ich warte (the bus I'm waiting for).
